newsitem.title: USA: U.S. offers $65 mln to stop mine near Yellowstone.
newsitem.headline: U.S. offers $65 mln to stop mine near Yellowstone.

text.p: The White House said Wednesday it had offered to pay Crown Butte Mines Inc. $65 million to stop the company from developing a proposed mine just outside Yellowstone National Park.
The $65 million will come from coal, oil and natural gas royalty revenue over several years from existing federal leases in Montana, the White House Council on Environmental Quality said.

The offer was made to carry out an agreement reached last August with Crown Butte to exchange assets worth up to $65 million for the New World Mine property to protect the Yellowstone and Clarks Fork rivers from mining pollution.

At the time, administration officials talked about exchanging land for the planned copper, gold and silver mining complex, but government and environmental officials said Wednesday the cash deal made more sense.

By giving Crown Butte money, the government would provide the company more certainty about the value of the exchange, instead of giving it another property which could be hit with future development restrictions.
At the same time, the administration would avoid trading one potential environmental mess for another on different property.
"There was some real difficulty in identifying federal properties that were non-controversial," said Tom Cassidy, general counsel for the environmental group American Rivers.

"With the transfer of a revenue stream from existing (oil and mineral) leases, it means that the problem that the Yellowstone and Clarks Fork rivers faced will not be faced by any other community," he said.
Crown Butte, which is partly owned by Canadian company Noranda Inc, has 30 days to agree to the plan. The company said it was pleased to receive the offer and was reviewing whether to accept it.

While Council on Environmental Quality chair Kathleen McGinty called the agreement "a good deal for taxpayers, for Crown Butte, and everyone who cares about Yellowstone," the plan could hit a snag in Congress, which must approve it.
House lawmakers complained about the government giving up $65 million in royalty revenue from federal leases in Montana.

"These assets belong to American taxpayers, and it is the responsibility of the Congress to see to it that dangerous precedents are not set in a mad rush to fulfill campaign promises," said House Appropriations Chairman Bob Livingston, a Louisiana Republican.

Lawmakers also voiced concern about the White House's plan to offset the $65 million loss by delaying the enrollment of 2 million acres of land into the Conservation Reserve Program, which pays farmers not to plant on fragile land.
"If they're going to try to solve the problem on the backs of farmers, we'd like to see it done without harming them," said Matt Raymond, spokesman for Sen. Conrad Burns, a Montana Republican.
Burns slammed the agreement, saying the administration could have saved taxpayers $65 million if it had determined through a normal environmental review that the mine should not be approved.
Congress must endorse the entire plan, partly to ensure that Montana will not lose its share of royalties from the federal leases to be used to pay Crown Butte.
